claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS (AWS-only).
AWS CDK allows developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem infrastructure, while AWS CDK is AWS-only.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, whereas Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because CDK is slowed by CloudFormation and Pulumi executes directly.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
With AWS CDK, secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, whereas Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
CDK and CloudFormation act as code generators producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, without generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments supports advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, deploying constructs/components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST v3 (Ion) has been or will be released as the stable version; as of the post's update date this statement says Ion is not yet stable.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST was originally built on top of AWS CDK and moved to Pulumi due to CDK/CloudFormation limitations and a need for multi-cloud/on-premises support.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account, not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of SST.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.
The SST team has said repeatedly, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST docs 'What is SST' say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

SST's published platform/package.json depends on @pulumi/pulumi plus Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (@pulumi/pulumi, @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls, @pulumiverse/vercel).
The SST repository is at anomalyco/sst, formerly sst/sst.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge translates each resource into cloud API calls via Terraform-bridged providers.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine.

Nitric's docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments," and official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers. Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.

Defang's pulumi-defang README describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`"; Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (stars) than SST itself.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed and its release cadence hasn't changed as a result of the team's attention on opencode.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code enables guardrails enforced centrally; components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
SST users are running Pulumi's engine and could adopt Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components without leaving the engine they already use.
The blog post at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
The docs page /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ exists and explains the engine mechanics.

Linked pages exist: /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/.
SST is a strong fit for an opinionated, full-stack application framework, and does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across applications.
